To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a high proportion of patients with stroke and transient ischemic attack (TIA) are discharged with an incorrect diagnosis, 2) a high proportion are not admitted to hospital at all, and 3) a high proportion have an incorrect diagnosis when admitted.
hospital discharge codes were a valid and efficient method for identifying incident stroke cases.

(1) the use of hospital discharge data for stroke surveillance can be improved by using a more comprehensive set of ICD codes; and (2) the use of ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes is not a major problem in the identification of stroke patients, but the use of the more specific ICD-10 stroke codes can improve the identification of stroke subtypes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of incident stroke events from hospital discharge data.
the identification of the most important causes of stroke in the elderly.
the use of the hospital discharge database in the study of stroke incidence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no significant differences in the prevalence of the various types of strokes between men and women.
hospital discharge data is a good source for identifying incident strokes in the population.
there is a strong association between the use of statins in patients with stroke and the incidence of recurrent stroke.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have identified a number of factors that are associated with a higher risk for developing stroke, and that the risk of developing stroke is increased in patients with a previous diagnosis of hypertension, diabetes, and atrial fibrillation.
we have identified a new mechanism of how to induce a stroke in a mouse model of cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA).

we identified a large number of stroke cases in the Norwegian population, and that we found that the hospital discharge register underestimates the number of stroke cases, but the underestimation was not as large as previously described in other countries.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of hospitalization records as a source for identifying incident stroke is not recommended.
there are several ways to identify stroke in a population-based setting, but the most accurate is the use of a validated stroke register.
we have shown that the use of hospital discharge data for stroke incidence is feasible in Norway.
